analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to exclude land from endangered species critical habitat protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in March 2014 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how the government protects habitat for endangered species. Today, agencies may exclude an area from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of protection; this bill would require them to do so, with only one exception — when leaving the area unprotected would drive the species extinct [S2][S3]. It would also require agencies to publish a quantitative economic analysis, covering land uses, property values, jobs, and state and local revenues, at the same time they propose a habitat designation [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee and never advanced [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners, developers, and resource industries (such as ranching, timber, mining, and oil and gas) whose land use plans are constrained by critical habitat designations. Making exclusions mandatory and putting an economic analysis out with every proposed designation would give these interests more grounds to shrink or block habitat protections that limit what they can do with land [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior or Commerce Secretary to exclude an area from critical habitat whenever the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of inclusion, unless exclusion would cause the species' extinction; current law makes such exclusion optional [S2][S3].

Requires a draft quantitative economic analysis — covering land and property values, employment, and state and local revenues — to be published for public comment alongside every proposed critical habitat designation [S2][S3].
Supporters argued this would give communities and affected landowners earlier and clearer information about the economic effects of habitat designations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Endangered and threatened species, which would lose habitat protection in any area where an economic case for exclusion can be made, and the public that benefits from functioning ecosystems and from the current, more protective standard. Wildlife conservation depends on habitat; mandatory exclusions make it harder to protect the places species need to recover [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Converting optional exclusions into mandatory ones would weaken the Endangered Species Act's habitat tool: land could be left unprotected whenever an economic benefit argument exists, with extinction as the only backstop [S2][S3].

Releasing a quantitative economic analysis at the proposal stage — before the final designation — could push agencies toward smaller designations, and habitat loss carries long-term public costs, from degraded ecosystems to lost recreational and commercial value, that a project-by-project economic analysis does not capture.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that agencies already weigh economics in habitat decisions and often exclude areas voluntarily, so the bill's main practical effect would be to shift the default toward less protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency gain — a public economic analysis with each proposed designation — is modest, since agencies already produce economic analyses for critical habitat rules. The bigger change is the mandatory exclusion requirement, which weakens habitat protection for species whose recovery depends on specific places. Weighed against a one-time increase in disclosure, the bill's main effect would be to favor land users over conservation, and it never advanced far enough to test that tradeoff [S2][S3][S5].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Pryor and Sen. Mary Landrieu introduced the bill on March 5, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S3][S5].
No further action was recorded: the committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill for a Senate vote, and it expired at the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landowners, developers, and resource industries came out no worse and no better — the status quo they opposed remained. The public's existing habitat protections also remained intact, since a bill that would have made habitat exclusions mandatory never became law [S2][S3][S5].

for.name: Sen. Mark Pryor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Community Protection Act of 2014 in the Senate

for.name: Sen. Mary Landrieu
for.what_they_did: Joined Pryor in introducing the bill, per the bill's introduction clause

for.name: 2 Senate cosponsors (1 D, 1 R)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor in addition to the sponsor

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out, held no recorded markup, and never scheduled it for floor action

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan in a small way — a Democratic sponsor and co-introducer plus one Republican cosponsor [S4] — but with only three senators attached and no recorded votes, the record shows no clear partisan split on the bill itself.

industries.note: Critical habitat designations can restrict what landowners may build, farm, or clear, so mandatory exclusions and an up-front economic analysis would lighten those restrictions. The bill died, so their land-use constraints stayed as they were.

industries.industry: Resource extraction and agriculture (ranching, timber, mining, oil and gas)
industries.note: Habitat designations can limit grazing, drilling, logging, and mining on both private and public land; the bill would have made economic-benefit exclusions the default. Its failure left existing habitat protections in place.
